projects.name: Xinjiang (XUAR) — state labour-transfer programmes
projects.desc: The situation behind the UFLPA. Goods mined, produced or manufactured wholly or in part in the region, or by a listed entity, are presumed made with forced labour and barred from US import. Open the DHS Entity List for the named companies — that list is where this becomes locatable at company level.

projects.name: Turkmenistan — state-organised cotton harvest
projects.desc: Public-sector workers mobilised into the annual harvest under threat of dismissal. Documented by the Cotton Campaign and raised in the ILO supervisory system. Contrast with Uzbekistan, below.

projects.name: Uzbekistan — cotton harvest (systemic forced labour ended)
projects.desc: Included deliberately as a case that changed. After more than a decade of monitoring, third-party campaigning and ILO engagement, the systemic state-imposed forced labour in the cotton harvest was found to have ended and the international boycott was lifted in 2022. Read it as evidence that a decade of sustained pressure on one commodity in one country can work.

projects.name: Democratic Republic of the Congo — artisanal cobalt and copper
projects.desc: Cobalt appears on the US Department of Labor list of goods produced by child labour or forced labour from the DRC, alongside copper, gold, tin, tantalum and tungsten. Artisanal pits sit alongside industrial concessions and feed the same refiners.

projects.name: Côte d'Ivoire & Ghana — cocoa
projects.desc: Cocoa from both countries appears on the US Department of Labor list for child labour, and from Côte d'Ivoire for forced labour. The buyers are a small number of traders and manufacturers, which is what makes this one of the most traceable supply chains on the list. In this country: The larger producer of the two, and the larger share of the estimated 1.56 million children in cocoa work across both countries.

projects.name: Côte d'Ivoire & Ghana — cocoa
projects.desc: Cocoa from both countries appears on the US Department of Labor list for child labour, and from Côte d'Ivoire for forced labour. projects.name: South Asia — brick kilns
projects.desc: Bricks from India, Pakistan, Nepal, Bangladesh and Afghanistan appear on the US Department of Labor list. The structure is advance-payment debt bondage across a seasonal migration, with whole families working against a loan. Kilns are unusually visible from satellite imagery. In this country: Bonded labour in kilns is prosecutable under the 1976 Act; the release certificate from the District Magistrate is the bottleneck.

In this country: Exit permits removed for most workers and a non-discriminatory minimum wage introduced in 2020; monitoring organisations continue to document blocked transfers and withheld wages.

projects.name: Southeast Asia — forced-criminality scam compounds
projects.desc: People recruited with fake job offers, trafficked across borders and held in guarded compounds to run online fraud, with beatings and debt used as control. Recorded by UN human-rights bodies and by regional law enforcement. A relatively new pattern, and one where the victim is often also treated as an offender — which makes the non-punishment principle central. In this country: Compounds concentrated in border areas outside effective central control, which is what makes extraction so difficult.

projects.name: Brazil — employers on the 'lista suja'
projects.desc: Brazil publishes a public register of employers found by labour inspectors to have subjected workers to conditions analogous to slavery, with the employer, the state and the number of workers found. It is the most precisely locatable government dataset in this field anywhere — and the model other countries have not copied.

projects.name: Malaysia — palm oil and rubber gloves
projects.desc: Migrant workers on employer-tied permits with recruitment debt and retained passports. Several producers have been the subject of US withhold release orders, some later revoked after remediation — which makes this a useful case study in what remediation is actually required to look like.

projects.name: Distant-water fishing fleets
projects.desc: Crews kept at sea for months or years through transhipment at sea, unable to leave the workplace by definition. Documented across several national fleets by investigative journalism and vessel-tracking analysis. The relevant tools are AIS and port-state control records rather than any land register.

projects.name: North Korea — overseas contract labour
projects.desc: Workers dispatched abroad under state contracts with wages remitted to the state. Covered by UN Security Council measures and by the US Department of Labor list. The workers are in third countries, not at this point — the marker sits at the sending state.

projects.name: Mauritania — hereditary slavery
projects.desc: Descent-based slavery, criminalised in law and persisting in practice, with prosecutions rare and anti-slavery activists themselves prosecuted. One of the few contexts where the older meaning of the word is the accurate one.

projects.name: Top Glove — disposable gloves
projects.desc: WRO issued 15 July 2020 on gloves from Top Glove and TG Medical, escalated to a Finding, on indicators including recruitment-fee debt bondage among migrant workers. The company reimbursed recruitment fees and the order was modified. The clearest documented instance anywhere of an import ban putting money back into workers' hands — which is why it is on this map alongside the open cases.

projects.name: FGV Holdings — palm oil
projects.desc: WRO of 30 September 2020 covering palm oil and palm-oil products from FGV Holdings, its subsidiaries and joint ventures. CBP announced a modification on 15 January 2026. Palm oil passes through refiners and traders before it reaches a brand, so the trade-data lens is where this becomes actionable downstream.

projects.name: Sime Darby Plantation — palm oil
projects.desc: WRO of 30 December 2020, following a petition by Liberty Shared rather than a government investigation. CBP cited information indicating all eleven ILO forced-labour indicators. The route worth noting: an NGO petition, evidence on recruitment fees and document retention, then a ban.

projects.name: Taepyung Salt Farm — sea salt
projects.desc: WRO of 3 April 2025, following long-documented exploitation of workers with disabilities on South Korean salt farms. South Korea was one of four countries newly added to the 2024 US list of goods — a reminder that these determinations are not confined to low-income producing countries.

projects.name: Linglong International Europe — tyres
projects.desc: WRO of 18 December 2025. Notable because the workplace is inside Europe and the workers were Vietnamese nationals recruited for a manufacturing and construction site. The corridor pattern — recruited far away, indebted before arrival, isolated on site — does not stop at the EU border.

projects.name: Giant Manufacturing — bicycles
projects.desc: WRO of 24 September 2025 against one of the world's largest bicycle manufacturers, on indicators affecting migrant workers. Worth sitting with: a listed producer can be a well-known consumer brand rather than an anonymous subcontractor.

projects.name: Zhen Fa 7 — fishing vessel
projects.desc: WRO of 28 May 2025 on seafood from a single named vessel. At sea the unit of enforcement is the boat, not the company, which is why the flag and IMO registries matter as much as any corporate registry — and why AIS behaviour, months at sea without a port call, is what usually surfaces one of these. Placed at the flag state rather than at sea: a vessel can only be acted against through the registry it flies under and the port it enters, so that is the jurisdiction worth knowing.

projects.name: Da Wang — fishing vessel
projects.desc: WRO of 18 August 2020, later escalated to a Finding, which allows seizure rather than only detention. One of several Taiwan-affiliated vessels named from 2019, alongside Yu Long No. 2 (11 May 2020) and Lien Yi Hsing No. 12 (31 December 2020). Placed at the flag state rather than at sea: a vessel can only be acted against through the registry it flies under and the port it enters, so that is the jurisdiction worth knowing.

projects.name: Marange diamond fields
projects.desc: Rough diamonds from the Marange fields have been barred from US entry since the order of 30 September 2019, on evidence of forced labour in mining. A field-wide rather than company-wide order, which is the form these take where the production is not organised under oneoperator.

projects.name: Eastern DRC — artisanal gold
projects.desc: WRO of 30 September 2019 covering gold from artisanal small mines in eastern DRC. Issued the same day as orders on Marange diamonds, Malaysian rubber gloves from WRP Asia Pacific, and bone char from Brazil — five orders in one day, which remains the largest single action of its kind.

projects.name: Turkmenistan — cotton, country-wide order
projects.desc: One of the few orders covering an entire country's output of a commodity: cotton produced anywhere in Turkmenistan has been barred from US entry since 18 May 2018, following a petition filed by the International Labor Rights Forum in April 2016. The harvest is state-mobilised, which is what makes a country-wide order the only coherent form.
